title: How to Build a Retirement Plan When You’re a High Earner in the U.S.
description: Advanced tax strategies for the 'Henrys' (High Earners, Not Rich Yet).
content:
Being a high earner ($200k+ individual, $400k+ household) solves many cash flow problems but introduces massive tax inefficiencies. The standard advice of 'Max your 401(k) and Roth IRA' doesn't work because you are phased out of direct Roth contributions and the $23,000 401(k) limit is too small to maintain your lifestyle in retirement. To build wealth efficiently at this level, you must move beyond basic accounts to advanced structures like the Mega Backdoor Roth, NQDC plans, and Taxable Brokerage optimization.

Key Takeaways

  • The Savings Rate Trap: High earners often suffer from lifestyle creep. Saving 10% of $400k is not enough to replace a $400k lifestyle. You need to aim for a 30-40% savings rate.
  • The Mega Backdoor Roth: If your employer allows 'After-Tax' contributions, you can stuff an additional ~$46,000 into your 401(k) annually above the standard limit. This is the most powerful tool for high earners.
  • Asset Location is Mandatory: With a 37% federal tax rate, holding bonds or REITs in a taxable account is a disaster. You must be surgical about placing tax-inefficient assets in tax-deferred accounts.
  • NQDC Plans: Deferred Compensation plans allow you to defer 50%+ of your salary to lower your current tax bracket, paying taxes only when you withdraw in retirement.

Why It Matters (US Context)

High earners are hit by the 'Net Investment Income Tax' (3.8%) and 'Additional Medicare Tax' (0.9%). Efficient planning isn't just about growth; it's about avoiding the 50% combined marginal tax rate trap in states like California or New York.

The High-Income Waterfall

You need more buckets than the average saver.

1. The Basic Max-Out

401(k): $23,000 (Pre-Tax). Lowers your top-line AGI.
HSA: $4,300 (Family $8,550). The only deduction left available to you.

2. The 'Backdoor' Strategies

Backdoor Roth IRA: You can't contribute directly. You must contribute $7,000 to a Traditional IRA (Non-Deductible) and convert it immediately.
Mega Backdoor Roth: Call your 401(k) provider. Ask if you can make 'After-Tax' contributions and do 'In-Service Withdrawals'. If yes, you can funnel tens of thousands more into Roth.

3. The Taxable Overflow

Once tax-advantaged space is full ($70k+), the rest goes to a Brokerage account.
Strategy: Buy Municipal Bonds (MUB) for tax-free income and broad ETFs (VTI) for low turnover. Avoid active funds that generate capital gains distributions.

Executive Compensation Tactics

  1. RSU Management: If you get Restricted Stock Units, sell them the moment they vest. Treat them as a cash bonus. Don't hold a concentrated position in your employer; your job is already enough risk there.
  2. Deferred Comp (NQDC): If eligible, defer salary to lower your bracket today. Schedule payouts to start 5 years after retirement when your tax rate drops.
  3. Umbrella Insurance: High net worth makes you a target for lawsuits. Get a $2M-$5M umbrella policy. It costs ~$300/year and protects your nest egg.
  4. Tax Loss Harvesting: Use a robo-advisor or DIY to aggressively harvest losses in the taxable account. A $3,000 deduction saves you $1,100 in taxes at top brackets.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Whole Life Insurance good for high earners?

Agents push it as a 'tax shelter', but fees are huge. Usually, maxing out a Taxable Brokerage account with tax-efficient ETFs outperforms Whole Life. Use it only as a bond substitute for the ultra-wealthy ($10M+).

Can I deduct student loan interest?

No. At your income level, that deduction phases out. You have to pay loans with raw, after-tax dollars.

What is the AMT?

Alternative Minimum Tax. It removes many deductions (like state taxes). If you have lots of ISO stock options, you need a CPA to plan for the AMT hit.
